newsitem.title: USA: Jobless claims rise in latest week.
newsitem.headline: Jobless claims rise in latest week.

text.p: The number of people filing new claims for unemployment benefits in the holiday-shortened Fourth of July week rose by 40,000, the government said on Thursday, driven in part by normal automobile industry retooling layoffs.

The Labour Department said 377,000 people filed first-time claims for unemployment insurance benefits in the week ended July 5, up from 337,000 claims in the previous week, but below Wall Street's forecast of 341,000 claims.
In the prior two years, when automobile layoffs occurred in the week including the July 4 holiday, unadjusted claims rose by similar amounts, Labour said.
First time claims were also at their highest since 403,000 people filed in the week ended March 30, 1996, the department said.

The rise brought the average weekly rate of new claims over the past four weeks -- a more accurate measurement of employment trends than the more-volatile weekly numbers -- to 348,500, up from 339,000.

Total benefit rolls rose 159,000 to reach 2.478 million in the week ended June 28, the latest period for which those figures were available. That was up from 2.319 million the prior week, the department said.
Labour said five states reported increases in claims of more than a 1,000, unadjusted, in the June 28 week, the latest week for which those data were available.
They were Michigan, with 6,337 additional claims, Massachusetts, with 3,481, Virginia, with 2,626, New York, with 2,416 and New Jersey, with 2,366.

Michigan cited layoffs for model changeovers in the automobile industry. Massachusetts had layoffs in the service industry, while New York and New Jersey had layoffs in transportation and service industries.
Virginia reported layoffs in the transportation equipment, textile, furniture, rubber and chemical industies.
Three states reported decreases in initial claims exceeding 1,000, unadjusted, in the June 28 week.
They were Pennsylvania, with 3,783 fewer claims, Ohio, with 1,421 and Oregon, with 1,084.
Pennsylvania cited fewer layoffs in the transportation equipment, transportation, trade and service industries. Ohio and Oregon had no comment.
